assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks (Lamb-Dicke trapping of neutral atoms at the magic wavelength, then Sr and Yb clocks at the 1e-18 level) transformed time and frequency metrology, and provide a precision platform for tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and searches for new physics. The idea is original, clear and conceptually elegant, and the impact is broad across atomic physics.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and first demonstrated it; Ye led the extension to record stability and accuracy, many-body (Fermi-degenerate) clocks and systematic control. This is a clean two-person configuration. Contributions of others (e.g. Sr and Yb groups at NIST, PTB, Paris, JILA) are real but secondary to the original scheme and its ultimate performance.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed by many laboratories over two decades; clock comparisons have repeatedly improved and redefinition of the SI second is under discussion. Recognition is timely, especially since the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured adjacent precision-spectroscopy and ion-trap work.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views the contribution as sufficiently distinct from the earlier frequency-comb (2005) and trapped-ion-control (2012) prizes.
Some credit for the lattice-clock concept is shared with other proposers (for example early magic-wavelength and Sr-clock ideas), which I cannot fully verify from the supplied text.
Jun Ye also appears in the ultracold-molecule candidate, so any prize configuration across candidates should be coordinated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation of Hubbard models with ultracold atoms (Mott-insulator transition in optical lattices, then single-site resolved quantum gas microscopes and fermionic Hubbard physics) made strongly correlated lattice models directly controllable and observable. The conceptual originality is high and it created a field bridging atomic physics and condensed matter.
assessment.attribution: The Jaksch-Zoller theoretical proposal, the Greiner-Hansch-Bloch experiment and the later microscope and Fermi-Hubbard work are the decisive steps; Zoller, Bloch and Greiner capture theory, the founding experiment and the single-site microscope era. Cirac, Jaksch and others contributed heavily to theory, and the quantum gas microscope also involved several groups (Harvard, MPQ), so the fair split is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Experiments are reproducible in dozens of groups and the techniques are mature. Quantitative quantum simulation of open problems such as the Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram is still developing, which makes the claim of a settled scientific payoff somewhat incomplete, though the methodological discovery is secure.
uncertainties: Overlap with Bose-Einstein condensation (2001) and with the Cirac-Zoller candidate leads to a risk of an unfair partitioning of credit.
The scientific result for strongly correlated models is still emerging; the discovery is mostly an enabling technique.
Choice among Bloch, Greiner, Cirac and Zoller as the three is uncertain; Cirac is omitted here but could plausibly replace one.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened an entirely new platform for correlated and topological phases with a tunable twist angle; the flat-band prediction and experimental observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity are original, striking and have spawned moire materials as a field.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the flat-band prediction at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group (with Yuan Cao as first author, who is not in the credited list) observed the correlated insulator and superconductivity. The supplied names cover theory and experiment, but a student first-author contribution and other groups (e.g. Dean, Young, Efetov, Yazdani) complicate attribution.
assessment.maturity: Discovery dates to 2018 and has been replicated widely, but the nature of the superconducting pairing and the correlated states is still being debated. Recognition might be somewhat early for a field still unfolding.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism and correlated phases are not settled.
Credit for the experimental discovery is spread over several groups and includes a junior first author outside the credited names.
Possible premature timing relative to eventual clarity.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and the experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells, established a new topological classification of band insulators with robust edge/surface states. This is among the most important condensed-matter discoveries of recent decades.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the Z2 and quantum spin Hall predictions; Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposed HgTe, and Molenkamp's group observed the effect. Hasan's group observed three-dimensional topological insulators (Bi-Sb, Bi2Se3) and is also credited, as is Zhang, who is not on the list and is deceased. The three-person configuration of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is plausible but leaves out the three-dimensional experimental side.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: confirmed by many independent groups and materials, with extensive follow-up (ARPES, transport, magnets). Timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Recognition of three-dimensional topological insulators (Hasan, Moore, Fu) versus two-dimensional quantum spin Hall experiments leaves unresolved allocation.
Contributions of Bernevig, Hughes and the late Shoucheng Zhang are not representable in the credited list.
Overlaps with other topological candidates, which could split the credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics implemented strong coupling of a superconducting qubit to a single microwave photon in an on-chip resonator, giving the dominant architecture for superconducting quantum processors and for studying light-matter interaction in a new regime. It is original and has major technological and fundamental impact. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, and this is a natural continuation.
assessment.attribution: The Blais-Huang-Wallraff-Girvin-Schoelkopf proposal and the Wallraff et al. 2004 demonstration were decisive. Girvin is a major theorist in the same work and four names are credited; with three allowed, one of Blais or Girvin must be left out, which is an uncomfortable allocation. Schoelkopf and Wallraff are the clear experimental leaders.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced in many laboratories, with the architecture used throughout superconducting quantum computing. Mature as a physics discovery, though one may worry that recognition is soon after the 2025 award in the same area.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would honour superconducting circuits again so soon after 2025.
Theory credit between Blais and Girvin, and the roles of the Yale and Saclay precursor work.
Quantum-computing hardware claims should not be conflated with the physics discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Detection of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and the observation of a neutrino source (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, Galactic plane) opened neutrino astronomy using a cubic-kilometre Antarctic ice detector. This is an original, large-scale instrument achievement with clear discovery physics.
assessment.attribution: Halzen was the intellectual driver of the IceCube concept and Karle a key figure in the construction and scientific programme, but this was a collaboration of hundreds, and AMANDA predecessors and other leaders (e.g. Yoshida, Kowalski, Resconi, Ahrens) matter. Yoshida is also credited but I propose the two-person core; the fair allocation of credit within a large collaboration is a real issue.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is firmly established; source identification is at the 4-5 sigma level and the origin of the flux is not yet understood. Reasonably mature for the detection, but not for the astrophysical interpretation.
uncertainties: Collaboration credit is diffuse and the individual leadership roles are hard to adjudicate.
Identification of sources and the interpretation of the flux are still developing.
Whether the Nobel Committee would see this as physics rather than astronomy given the overlap with the 2002 neutrino prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave coherence into precision sensors for gravity, rotation and fundamental constants and tests of the equivalence principle. Its conceptual basis is clear, and it connects to laser cooling work already honoured, but its fundamental discovery content is less sharp than other candidates.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's theory of light-pulse interferometry, Pritchard's first atom interferometers with gratings and Kasevich/Chu's light-pulse gravimeter are the key steps. The credited names are plausible, but Chu is not in the list and Chu's 1997 prize overlaps; Ertmer, Mlynek, Keith and Carnal are also relevant historical contributors.
assessment.maturity: Mature as a technique with commercial gravimeters, but ambitious applications such as gravitational-wave detection and dark-matter searches are not yet realised.
uncertainties: Overlap with Steven Chu's laser-cooling prize and unclear separation of credit.
Whether the main impact is metrology rather than a new fundamental discovery.
Priority of Bordé versus Kasevich and Chu is not fully certain from supplied evidence.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade and programmable neutral-atom arrays make strongly interacting quantum many-body systems and quantum simulators/processors with individually controlled atoms. The atomic physics of Rydberg states is physically rich, and the platform has produced striking demonstrations of quantum phases and high-fidelity gates.
assessment.attribution: The blockade proposal (Jaksch, Lukin et al.), early blockade demonstrations (Grangier, Browaeys, Saffman) and the optical-tweezer array experiments (Lukin, Browaeys, Bernien) are all credited, with four names listed. A three-person prize leaves out either Grangier or one of the main players, and the original theory proposal of Jaksch et al. is not fully represented.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly developing and independently reproduced by several groups, but error-corrected computing and long-term payoff are not yet demonstrated. Probably early compared with the other atomic candidates.
uncertainties: Allocation among four credited names, with important theory proposers missing from the credited list.
Maturity: the field is moving fast and the lasting interpretation is not yet fixed.
Overlap with the Hubbard quantum-simulation candidate and with Lukin appearing in several candidates.
